sets.title: RC: The Police, the Law and the Citizen
sets.context:
[Passage paraphrased from the original]
Maintaining order in abnormal times is the army's role, but in normal times another force - the police - makes citizens obey the law and act with due regard to the rights of others, and it protects the lives and property of law-abiding people. Laws exist to keep citizens personally safe, to prevent murder and violent crime, to secure citizens' property against theft and damage, and to protect the right of communities and castes to carry out their 'customs and ceremonies' - but only so long as these do not conflict with the rights of others. The good citizen obeys such laws of his own free will, taking care that what he does respects the rights and well-being of others; the bad citizen is 'restrained' from breaking them only by fear of the consequences of his actions, and it is this force that takes the necessary steps to compel him to behave like a good citizen. The supreme control of law and order in a state rests with a Minister who is responsible to the State Assembly and acts through the Inspector-General of Police.

sets.title: RC: Brain Drain or Brain Bank?
sets.context:
[Passage paraphrased from the original]
A News Week report notes that in American colleges, students of Asian origin - many of them Indian - outperform not just other minority groups but the white majority too, an achievement worth being proud of. Since these talented students are unlikely to return to India, commentators once called this the 'brain drain' problem. Recently, however, policymakers have begun preferring the term 'brain bank' instead of 'brain drain', arguing that the expertise of Indians abroad is merely deposited elsewhere, not lost forever.
That may be true, but a brain bank, like any other bank, mainly serves customers in its own neighbourhood - so the skills of these excelling Asian students will chiefly benefit the USA. Whatever non-resident Indians do for India (or their counterparts do for other Asian countries) is only a side effect, however significant.
It is worth asking why Indians perform so much better abroad. The very same students News Week praises would likely have had very different outcomes had they studied in India. In America they found elbow room, books, and facilities unavailable and unlikely to become available at home. Having to prove themselves in a new country, and facing competition of an international standard, must have shaken off mental and physical laziness. But these other advantages of America could be recreated here too, if our social attitudes - especially toward youth - were to change.
We need to value individuals and their unique qualities over mere conformity and respectability. We need to learn the language of encouragement, not just polish our skill in flattery.

So 'colours sky high' should code to the set {ki, la, jo} - which is exactly the set of codes in options (c) and (d), just in different order, not option (e). Keeping the answer key's marked option (e) as given.

questions.question:
Statements: W ≥ D < M < P < A = F
Conclusions:
I. F > D
II. P < W
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: From D < M < P < A = F, we get F > D directly, so I follows. There is no direct chain linking P and W (W ≥ D is a separate branch from D < M < P), so II does not follow. Only conclusion I follows.

questions.question:
Statements: H ≥ M > F < A = B > S
Conclusions:
I. H > B
II. F < S
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: The chain has a 'valley' at F (M > F < A), which breaks the link between the H/M side and the A/B/S side, so H vs B cannot be compared - I does not follow. Similarly F and S sit on opposite sides of the valley with no direct link, so II does not follow. Neither conclusion follows.

questions.question:
Statements: B > T > Q > R = F
Conclusions:
I. Q ≥ F
II. T > F
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: Q > R = F gives Q > F strictly, so the weaker conclusion 'Q ≥ F' is treated as not following (only the exact relation Q > F holds). T > Q > R = F gives T > F directly, so II follows. Only conclusion II follows.

questions.question:
Statements: S = R ≥ Q, P < Q
Conclusions:
I. S ≥ P
II. R > P
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: Combining, S = R ≥ Q > P. This gives R > P directly, so II follows. S ≥ P is treated as not following because the derived relation between S and P is the strict form (S > P via R), not a genuine ≥ ambiguity. Only conclusion II follows.

questions.question:
Statements: S ≥ M < Y = Z > F > T
Conclusions:
I. S > F
II. Y > T
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
questions.explanation: The chain has a valley at M (S ≥ M < Y), so S cannot be compared with Y, Z, F or T - I does not follow. Y = Z > F > T gives Y > T directly, so II follows. Only conclusion II follows.

questions.question:
Conclusions:
I. Dancer can be player being a possibility.
II. All those dancers who are footballers are also music lovers.
III. Any cricketer can never be player.
questions.explanation: Dancers exclude cricketers and cricketers exclude players, but dancers and players are not directly linked, so a dancer being a player remains a valid possibility (I follows). Every footballer is both a dancer and a music lover, so any dancer who is a footballer is automatically a music lover (II follows). 'No cricketer is player' is a direct premise, so III follows. All three follow.

questions.question:
Conclusions:
I. All cricketers can be music lovers.
II. Some players are footballers.
III. At least some footballers are cricketers.
questions.explanation: Since footballers are entirely contained in dancers, and no dancer is a cricketer, footballers and cricketers are completely disjoint - so III (some footballers are cricketers) does not follow. Nothing links players and footballers directly, so II does not follow for certain. Music lover is only tied to footballers, not excluded for cricketers, so it remains a possibility that all cricketers are music lovers - I follows as a possibility. Only I follows.

questions.question:
Conclusions:
I. 36% of girls are intelligent.
II. 2% of girls are intelligent.
III. Some boys can never be a girl.
questions.explanation: 'Very few girls are intelligent' is a vague quantifier compatible with a range of small percentages, so both 36% and 2% remain valid possibilities - I and II follow. Boys and girls are not stated to be mutually exclusive categories anywhere in the four given statements, so III cannot be concluded from them alone. Both I and II follow.

questions.question:
Conclusions:
I. All leaders are professors.
II. There is a possibility that every girl can be a professor.
III. All professors can be leaders.
questions.explanation: Since no girl is a leader but girls could still overlap with professors (nothing excludes it), it remains possible every girl is a professor - II follows as a possibility. Some professors are already stated to be leaders, so it remains possible (though not certain) that all professors are leaders - III follows as a possibility. 'All leaders are professors' is too strong a certainty to draw, so I does not follow. Both II and III follow.

questions.question:
Conclusions:
I. At least some professors are girls.
II. No professor is intelligent.
III. 5% of professors are leaders.
questions.explanation: Some professors are stated to be leaders and boys; nothing forces professors to include girls, so I does not follow for certain. Professors overlapping with boys (who are all intelligent) means 'no professor is intelligent' cannot be concluded, so II does not follow. Since some professors are leaders, a small percentage such as 5% remains a valid possibility, so III follows. Only III follows.

questions.question:
How is J related to K?
I. J's father P is the brother of N. N is K's wife.
II. J is the son of P. P is the brother of N. N is K's wife.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary
questions.explanation: Statement I only tells us J is P's child (gender unknown), so J could be N's/K's nephew or niece - not sufficient alone. Statement II additionally specifies J is P's son, fixing J's gender, so J is definitely K's nephew (N being K's wife, P being N's brother). Statement II alone is sufficient.

questions.question:

questions.explanation: Statement I gives a range of 4-8 days; statement II gives a range of 8-10 days. Neither range alone pins down a single value, but the only day common to both ranges is 8, so both statements together are necessary and sufficient.

questions.question:
How is the word 'GATES' coded in the code language?
I. 'BRICK' is coded as 'LDJSC' and 'PIN' is coded as 'OJQ'
II. 'WATER' is coded as 'SFUBX' and 'DISH' is coded as 'ITJE'
options: Statement I alone is sufficient, but statement II alone is not sufficient
Statement II alone is sufficient, but statement I alone is not sufficient
Either statement I alone or statement II alone is sufficient
Both statements I and II together are not sufficient
Both statements I and II together are necessary
questions.explanation: The rule (verified independently from each statement) is: reverse the letters of the word, then shift each letter one place forward in the alphabet. From statement I: BRICK reversed is KCIRB, shifted +1 gives LDJSC (matches); PIN reversed is NIP, shifted +1 gives OJQ (matches). From statement II: WATER reversed is RETAW, shifted +1 gives SFUBX (matches); DISH reversed is HSID, shifted +1 gives ITJE (matches). Either statement alone reveals the same rule, so GATES can be coded from either one (reversed SETAG, shifted +1 = TFUBH). Either statement alone is sufficient.

questions.question: In Swartkans territory, archaeologists discovered charred bone fragments dating back one million years. Analysis of the fragments, which came from a variety of animals, showed that they had been heated to temperatures no higher than those produced in experimental campfires made from branches of white stinkwood, the most common tree around Swartkans. Which of the following, if true, would, together with the information above, provide the best basis for the claim that the charred bone fragments are evidence of the use of fire by early hominids?
options: The white stinkwood tree is used for building material by the present day inhabitants of Swartkans
Forest fires can heat wood to a range of temperatures that occur in campfires
The bone fragments were fitted together by the archaeologists to form the complete skeletons of several animals
The bone fragments were found in several distinct layers of limestone that contained primitive cutting tools known to have been used by early hominids
questions.explanation: The argument needs independent evidence directly linking early hominids to the bone fragments. Finding the fragments alongside primitive cutting tools known to be used by early hominids provides exactly that link, strengthening the claim that the charring was due to hominid use of fire.

questions.question: Statement: It has been reported in a recent research report that taller people are found to be happier than those who are relatively shorter. Which of the following contradicts the above finding?
options: People are generally truthful when they respond to the questions of such research studies
Those people who have a comfortable lifestyle are found to be happier than those who lead a strenuous lifestyle irrespective of their height
Shorter people suffer from inferiority complex throughout their life
Taller people are found to be more positive in approach to daily chores of life
questions.explanation: If happiness actually tracks lifestyle comfort regardless of height, then height itself is not the real driver of happiness, which contradicts the finding that taller people are happier because they are taller.

questions.question: Statement: Many patients suffering from malaria were administered anti-malarial drug for a week. Some of them did not respond to the traditional drug and their condition deteriorated after four days. Which of the following would weaken the findings mentioned in the above statement?

The mosquitoes carrying malaria are found to be resistant to traditional malarial drugs
Majority of the patients suffering from malaria responded well to the traditional malarial drugs and recovered from the illness
Many drug companies have stopped manufacturing traditional malarial drugs
questions.explanation: If most patients actually responded well and recovered using the traditional drug, this weakens the implied suggestion that the traditional drug is generally ineffective against malaria.

questions.question: Statement: The cost of manufacturing cars in state A is 30% less than the cost of manufacturing cars in state B. Even after transportation fee for the differential distances of states A and B and the interstate taxes, it is cheaper to manufacture cars in state B than state A for selling these cars in state C. Which of the following supports the conclusion drawn in the above statement?
options: The cost of transportation from state A to state C is more than 30% of the production cost
The production costs of cars in state B are lower in comparison to state A
Only Entry Tax at state C is more for the products originated in state A
Entry Tax at state C is more for the products originated in state B
The total of transportation cost of cars from state B to state C and Entry Tax of cars at state C is less than 30% of the production cost of cars in state B
questions.explanation: If transporting from A to C costs more than the entire 30% saving A has over B, that overhead wipes out A's cost advantage, directly supporting the claim that manufacturing in B works out cheaper for selling in C.

questions.question: Statement: There was a slow decline in the number of patients with flu-like symptoms visiting various health facilities in the city during the last fortnight. Which of the following substantiates the facts mentioned in the above statement?
options: Majority of the people suffering from flu visit the health facilities in the city

questions.explanation: Checking each: (a) W+T-H makes W the brother of T, T the father of H, so W is H's uncle, not grandfather. None of the given codes produce 'grandfather' (a father-of-father chain using '-' twice), so the answer is None of these.

questions.explanation: Checking each: (b) R÷T-M makes R the mother of T and T the father of M, so R is M's grandmother, not aunt. (c) R×T÷M×J makes R the sister of T, T the mother of M, and M the sister of J - this makes R the (maternal) aunt of M, but the last clause fixes M as female (sister of J), making M a niece, not a nephew. (d) R÷T-M+J makes R the grandmother of M and J. None of the codes give a male M as the nephew of R, so the answer is None of these.

questions.question: How is T related to S in 'W ÷ T – H + V – S'?
questions.explanation: W÷T means W is mother of T; T–H means T is father of H; H+V means H is brother of V; V–S means V is father of S. So T is H's and V's father, making T the (paternal) grandfather of S. 'Grandfather' is not among the listed options (sister/mother/aunt/uncle), so the answer is None of these.

questions.question: What does the expression 'S ÷ T – H × V – N' mean?
options: S is great grandmother of N
questions.explanation: S÷T: S is mother of T. T–H: T is father of H. H×V: H is sister of V. V–N: V is father of N. So T is father of siblings H and V, and S (T's mother) is grandmother of H and V; since V is N's father, S is N's great-grandmother.

questions.explanation: Let tens digit = y, units digit = x, with y > x. From I: y - x = 5. From II: y + x = 7. Solving together: y=6, x=1, giving the number 61. Neither statement alone fixes a unique number; both together are necessary.

questions.question:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence; the letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error, the answer is (e).
The P.M. said (a)/ that it was his decision (b)/ and that nobody (c)/ could get it changed. (d)/ No error (e)
questions.explanation: The second 'that' (before 'nobody') is superfluous when the clauses are joined by 'and' - it should read 'and nobody could get it changed'. The error is in part (c).

questions.question:
Each sentence below has two blank spaces. Choose the pair of words that fits both blanks, in sequence, to make the sentence grammatically correct.
The ___________ you work, the ___________ for your prosperity.
questions.explanation: This is a comparative construction ('The harder..., the better...'), matching the standard 'the more X, the more Y' pattern.

questions.question:
Each sentence below has two blank spaces. Choose the pair of words that fits both blanks, in sequence, to make the sentence grammatically correct.
___________ you need a duplicate ration card, you must submit the ___________ of your residence.
questions.explanation: 'Should you need...' is a conditional inversion equivalent to 'If you need...', and 'proof of residence' is the correct standard phrase.

questions.question:
Each sentence below has two blank spaces. Choose the pair of words that fits both blanks, in sequence, to make the sentence grammatically correct.
It was my ___________ that ___________ to the serious problem.
questions.explanation: 'negligence' logically 'led to' a serious problem - this pairing fits both the meaning and the idiom ('led to a problem').

questions.question:
Each sentence below has two blank spaces. Choose the pair of words that fits both blanks, in sequence, to make the sentence grammatically correct.
Because he was ___________ he left the party earlier and ___________ home.
questions.explanation: 'unwell' explains leaving early, and 'returned home' is the natural, idiomatic completion.

questions.question:
Each sentence below has two blank spaces. Choose the pair of words that fits both blanks, in sequence, to make the sentence grammatically correct.
An impartial person ___________ others without any ___________ .
questions.explanation: An impartial person 'judges others without any bias' - this pairing directly reflects the meaning of 'impartial'.

questions.question:
Choose the phrase that should replace the bold/underlined phrase to make the sentence grammatically correct. If the sentence is already correct, choose 'No correction required'.
The Governor has a good collection of paintings adoring the walls of the Raj Bhavan.
questions.explanation: 'Adoring' (loving) is the wrong word here - the intended word is 'adorning' (decorating). 'Paintings adorning the walls' is correct.

questions.question:
Choose the phrase that should replace the bold/underlined phrase to make the sentence grammatically correct. If the sentence is already correct, choose 'No correction required'.
The principals and teachers at the selected English Medium School were contacted.
questions.explanation: 'select' (meaning choice/elite) is the intended word rather than 'selected', and 'at' is the correct preposition here, giving 'at the select English Medium School'.

questions.question:
Choose the phrase that should replace the bold/underlined phrase to make the sentence grammatically correct. If the sentence is already correct, choose 'No correction required'.
Besides these norms, the data was also analyzed to form the sub groups.
questions.explanation: 'Data' is treated as plural in formal usage, so it should take 'were', not 'was' - giving 'the data were also analyzed'.

questions.question:
Choose the phrase that should replace the bold/underlined phrase to make the sentence grammatically correct. If the sentence is already correct, choose 'No correction required'.
He does not know the Mount Everest is the Most highest mountain peak.
questions.explanation: 'Most highest' is a double superlative error; the correct superlative form is simply 'the highest mountain'.

questions.question:
Choose the phrase that should replace the bold/underlined phrase to make the sentence grammatically correct. If the sentence is already correct, choose 'No correction required'.
Walking in the morning in open air is being observed to be better for the health of the people who live in congestion.
questions.explanation: The original sentence is already grammatically correct as it stands - no correction is required.

questions.explanation: 'Delinking of jobs from degrees' is the correct idiomatic phrase (delink X from Y).

questions.question: Fill blank 117.
questions.explanation: 'One of the salient features' is the standard collocation with 'salient'.

questions.question: Fill blank 118.

questions.question: Fill blank 120.

questions.question: Fill blank 121.
questions.explanation: 'A flood of degree holders' conveys an overwhelming excess, matching the passage's point about devalued degrees.

questions.question: Fill blank 122.
questions.explanation: The number of students has been 'steadily rising', consistent with the earlier statement about a flood of degree holders.

questions.question: Fill blank 123.
questions.explanation: Graduates 'standing in queues' waiting for jobs is the idiomatic phrase for waiting in line for opportunities.

questions.question: Fill blank 124.

questions.question:
Rearrange P, Q, R, S between the fixed first and last sentences to form the most logical paragraph.
S1: There are numerous kinds of superstitions in different parts of the country.
P: But people go on respecting it through force of blind custom.
Q: Most of them have a bearing on 'luck' - good or bad.
R: Superstitions usually have their origin in fear and ignorance.
S: Nobody remembers now how a superstition first started in remote ages.
S6: A dog's howling predicts death - this is a typical superstition.
questions.explanation: Logical flow: Q follows S1 ('Most of them' refers back to the numerous superstitions - most concern luck) -> S (nobody now remembers how a superstition first started) -> P (yet people go on respecting it through blind custom) -> R (superstitions have their origin in fear and ignorance) -> S6 (typical example: a dog's howling predicts death). Sequence: QSPR.

questions.question:
Rearrange P, Q, R, S between the fixed first and last sentences to form the most logical paragraph.
S1: A spider's web, after a shower of rain, is a very beautiful thing.
P: This partly explains why spiders are thoroughly disliked.
Q: But no poet has ever sung of the beauty of the spiders, for most spiders are not beautiful.
R: On the contrary, most of them are rather unattractive, if not ugly!
S: Poets have sung about the beauty of the spider's webs, comparing the water drops on them to ropes of pearls.
S6: They are also feared because their bites may have unpleasant effects like a rash on the skin.
questions.explanation: Logical flow: S (poets praised the web's beauty) -> Q (but not the spiders themselves, which are not beautiful) -> R (in fact most are unattractive/ugly) -> P (this explains why spiders are disliked) -> S6 (also feared for their bites). Sequence: SQRP.

questions.question:
Rearrange P, Q, R, S between the fixed first and last sentences to form the most logical paragraph.
S1: Unhappiness and discontent spring not only from poverty.
P: Man is a strange creature fundamentally different from other animals.
Q: If they are undeveloped and unsatisfied, he may have all the comforts of wealth, but will still feel that life is not worthwhile.
R: He has far horizons, invariable hopes, spiritual powers.
S: What is missing in our age is the soul; there is nothing wrong with the body.
S6: We suffer from sickness of spirit and hence we should discover our roots in the internal.
questions.explanation: Logical flow: P (man is fundamentally different from animals) -> R (he has far horizons, hopes, spiritual powers) -> Q (if these remain undeveloped, wealth alone doesn't satisfy) -> S (what's missing is the soul, not the body) -> S6 (we suffer sickness of spirit, must look within). Sequence: PRQS.

questions.question:
Rearrange P, Q, R, S between the fixed first and last sentences to form the most logical paragraph.
S1: On vacation in Tangier, Morocco, my friend and I sat down at a street cafe.
P: At one point, he bent over with a big smile, showing me a single gold tooth and dingy fez.
Q: Soon I felt the presence of someone standing alongside me.
R: But this one wouldn't budge.
S: We had been cautioned about beggars and were told to ignore them.
S6: Finally a man walked over to me and whispered, 'Hey buddy... This guy is your waiter and he wants your order.'
questions.explanation: Logical flow: Q follows S1 (soon I felt someone standing alongside me) -> S (we had been cautioned about beggars and told to ignore them) -> R (but this one wouldn't budge) -> P (at one point he bent over with a big smile, showing a gold tooth) -> S6 (finally a man clarified he was the waiter). Sequence: QSRP.

questions.question:
Rearrange P, Q, R, S between the fixed first and last sentences to form the most logical paragraph.
S1: In 1934, William Golding published a small volume of poems.
P: During World War II (1939-45) he joined the Royal Navy and was present at the sinking of the Bismarck.
Q: He returned to teaching in 1945 and gave it up in 1962, and is now a full-time writer.
R: In 1939, he married and started teaching at Bishop Wordsworth's School in Salisbury.
S: At first his novels were not accepted.
S6: But 'Lord of the Flies', which came out in 1954, was welcomed as 'a most absorbing and instructive tale'.
questions.explanation: Logical flow (chronological): R (1939: married, started teaching) -> P (WWII service, 1939-45) -> Q (returned to teaching 1945, gave it up 1962, became a writer) -> S (at first his novels were rejected) -> S6 (but Lord of the Flies, 1954, was well received). Sequence: RPQS.

questions.question: The expression 'customs and ceremonies' means:
questions.explanation: In the context of communities and castes carrying out their 'customs and ceremonies', the phrase refers to their usual practices and religious rites.

questions.question: A suitable title for the passage would be:
options: the fear of the law and citizen's security
questions.explanation: The passage is centrally about the force (the police) that enforces laws in normal times, protects citizens and compels bad citizens to obey - so 'the functions of the police' is the apt title.

questions.question: Which of the following is not implied in the passage?
options: Law protects those who respect it
Law ensures people's religious and social rights absolutely and unconditionally
A criminal is deterred from committing crimes only for fear of the law
The forces of law help to transform irresponsible citizens into responsible ones
questions.explanation: The passage protects communal customs only 'so long as they do not conflict with the rights of others' - i.e., conditionally. So the claim that rights are ensured absolutely and unconditionally is NOT implied; the other statements are.

questions.question: According to the writer, which one of the following is not the responsibility of the police?
options: To protect the privileges of all citizens
To check violent activities of citizens
To ensure peace among citizens by safeguarding individual rights
To maintain peace during extraordinary circumstances
questions.explanation: The book's key marks (c). Note, however, that per the passage maintaining order in abnormal/extraordinary times is described as the army's role, so option (d) is also strongly arguable; the key's choice presumably reads 'safeguarding individual rights' as the job of the laws themselves rather than the police. Keeping the book's answer.

questions.question: Which of the following reflects the main thrust of the passage?
options: It deals with the importance of the army in maintaining law and order
It highlights the role of the police as superior to that of the army
It discusses the roles of the army and the police in different circumstances
It points to the responsibility of the Minister and the Inspector General of Police
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the army's role in abnormal times with the police's role in normal times - it discusses the roles of both in different circumstances.

questions.question: 'They are made to secure the property of citizens against theft and damage' means that the law:
options: helps in recovering the stolen property of the citizens
assists the citizens whose property has been stolen or destroyed
initiates process against offenders of law
safeguards people's possessions against being stolen or lost
questions.explanation: 'Secure property against theft and damage' means the law safeguards people's possessions from being stolen or lost - a protective (preventive) function, not recovery after the fact.

questions.question: Out of the following, which one has the opposite meaning to the word 'restrained' as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: 'Restrained' here means held back or checked; its opposite in this context is 'accelerated' (urged forward/speeded up), per the book's key. 'Inhibited' is a synonym, not an antonym.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is implied in the passage?
options: Peaceful citizens seldom violate the law, but bad citizens have to be restrained by the police
Criminals, who flout the law, are seldom brought to book
The police hardly succeed in converting bad citizens into good citizens
The police check the citizens, whether they are good or bad, and stop them from violating the law
questions.explanation: The book's key marks (d) - the force watches over all citizens and stops violations of the law. Note that option (a) also tracks the passage closely (good citizens obey freely, bad ones are restrained by fear); the key nonetheless prefers (d). Keeping the book's answer.

questions.question: Which of the following statements expresses most accurately the idea contained in the first sentence?
options: It is the job of the army to ensure internal peace at all times
It is the police that should always enforce law and order in the country
Army and the police ensure people's security through combined operations
It is in exceptional circumstances that the army has to ensure peace in the country
questions.explanation: The first sentence says the army maintains law and order in abnormal times - i.e., the army steps in only in exceptional circumstances.

questions.question: The last sentence of the passage implies that:
options: The Inspector General of Police is the sole authority in matters of law and order
In every State maintenance of public peace is under the overall control of the responsible Minister
A Minister and a responsible State Assembly exercise direct authority in matters pertaining to law and order
The Inspector General of Police is responsible to the State Assembly for maintaining law and order
questions.explanation: The last sentence places supreme control of law and order with a Minister (answerable to the State Assembly) who acts through the Inspector-General of Police - i.e., overall control rests with the responsible Minister.

questions.question: Among the many groups of students in American colleges, Asian students:
options: are often written about in magazines like News Week
have proved that they are as good as the whites
have only a minority status like the blacks
questions.explanation: The passage states Asian students outperform both other minority groups and the white majority, i.e. they have proved they are as good as (in fact better than) the whites.

questions.question: The students of Asian origin in America include:
options: persons from India who are very proud
Indians who are the most hard working of all
questions.explanation: The passage says 'many of these students must be of Indian origin', implying a fair/substantial number are Indian.

questions.question: In general, the talented young Indians studying in America:
options: have a reputation for being hard working
have the opportunity to contribute to India's development
can solve the brain drain problem because of recent changes in policy
will not return to pursue their careers in India
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says it is unlikely that these talented youngsters will come back to India - the familiar brain drain problem.

questions.question: There is talk now of the 'brain bank'. This idea:
options: is a solution to the brain drain problem
is a new problem caused partly by the brain drain
is a new way of looking at the role of qualified Indians living abroad
is based on a plan to utilize foreign exchange remittances to stimulate research and development
questions.explanation: 'Brain bank' is presented as a reframing - a new perspective on how to view the expertise of Indians settled abroad (deposited elsewhere, not lost), rather than a concrete solution or policy plan.

questions.question: The brain bank has limitations like all banks in the sense that:
options: a bank's services go mainly to those near it
small neighbourhood banks are not visible in this age of multinationals
only what is deposited can be withdrawn and utilized
no one can be forced to put his assets in a bank
questions.explanation: The passage compares the brain bank to an ordinary bank that 'primarily serves customers in its neighbourhood' - i.e. a bank's services mainly benefit those close to it (here, the USA rather than India).

questions.question: The author feels that what non-resident Indians do for India:
options: will have many useful side effects
will not be their main interest and concern
can benefit other Asian countries as a by-product
can American colleges be of service to the world community
questions.explanation: The passage says what NRIs do for India is 'only a by-product' - their main interest/concern lies with the country that benefits most from their skills (the USA), not India.

questions.question: The performance of Indians when they go to study in the West:
options: shows the fruits of hard work done by school teachers in India
should remind us that knowledge and wisdom are not limited by the boundaries of race and nation
is better than people in the West expect of non-whites
is better than what it would have been if they had studied in India
questions.explanation: The passage says these students 'would have probably had a very different tale' had they studied in India, given the better facilities, elbow room, and competition they found abroad - implying their performance is better than it would have been in India.

questions.question: The high level of competition faced by Asian students in America:
options: helps them overcome their lazy habits
makes them lazy since the facilities there are good
helps them prove that they are as good as whites
questions.explanation: The book's key marks (d). The passage's own wording ('competition ... must have cured mental and physical laziness') more directly supports option (a); the key nonetheless prefers (d), likely reading the competition as the mechanism by which they end up matching/outperforming white students. Keeping the book's answer.

questions.question: The author feels that some of the conditions other than the level of facilities that make the West attractive:
options: are available in India but young people do not appreciate them
can never be found here because we believe in conformity
can be created if our attitudes and values change
can also give respectability to our traditions and customs
questions.explanation: The passage says the other advantages found in America 'can be obtained here if we achieve a change in social attitudes' - i.e. they can be created if our attitudes and values change.

questions.question: One of the ways of making the situation in India better would be:
options: to eliminate flattery from public life
to distinguish between conformity and respectability
to give appreciation and not be tightfisted
to encourage people and not merely flatter them
questions.explanation: The book's key marks (c). This tracks the passage's closing call to 'value individuals ... more than conformity and respectability' and to 'learn the language of encouragement' rather than mere flattery - i.e. to be generous with genuine appreciation. Option (d) restates the same idea almost as closely; the key prefers (c). Keeping the book's answer.

questions.question: PM Narendra Modi launched which bank-linked digital initiative in India?
questions.explanation: In April 2015, PM Modi inaugurated ICICI Bank's 'Digital Village' initiative at Akodara in Gujarat, promoted as India's first fully digital village.

questions.question: LIC (Life Insurance Corporation of India) started its overseas business in which country?
questions.explanation: As per the answer key, LIC's overseas operations are recorded as having started in Bangladesh, one of the earliest countries where it opened business.

questions.question: Who was named the CEAT International Cricketer of the Year for 2015?
questions.explanation: Kumar Sangakkara, who had a standout 2015 World Cup with four consecutive centuries, was named CEAT International Cricketer of the Year in 2015.

questions.question: Where is Jim Corbett National Park located?
questions.explanation: Jim Corbett National Park, India's oldest national park, is located in Uttarakhand (Nainital district).

questions.question: The Omkareshwar Dam is located on which river?
questions.explanation: The Omkareshwar Dam is built across the Narmada river in Madhya Pradesh.

questions.question: Which country recently launched the first ATM with face recognition technology?
questions.explanation: Around 2015, Chinese banks piloted facial-recognition ATMs (using technology from firms such as Face++), making China the reported first mover on this front.

questions.question: What is the full form of BIOS?
questions.explanation: BIOS stands for Basic Input/Output System, the firmware used to perform hardware initialization during a computer's boot process.

questions.question: Agartala is the capital of which state?
questions.explanation: Agartala is the capital city of Tripura.

questions.question: Volkswagen Group and its subsidiaries form a ___________ multinational automotive manufacturing company.
questions.explanation: Volkswagen Group is a German multinational automotive manufacturer headquartered in Wolfsburg, Germany.

questions.question: In the Balance of Payments (BOP), unilateral transfer payments are included in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Unilateral transfers (gifts, remittances, donations) are recorded under the Current Account of the Balance of Payments, along with trade in goods and services and income flows.

questions.question: Who was selected as head coach of the India U-19 cricket team (around 2015)?
questions.explanation: Rahul Dravid was appointed head coach/mentor of the India Under-19 (and India A) cricket teams around this period.

questions.question: Where is the Katasraj temple located?
questions.explanation: The Katasraj (Katas Raj) temple complex is located in the Chakwal district of Punjab province, Pakistan.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of the Money Market?
questions.explanation: Treasury bills, commercial papers and certificates of deposit are classic short-term money market instruments; mutual funds are pooled investment vehicles that may invest across markets and are not themselves a money market instrument.

questions.question: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2014 was awarded to:
questions.explanation: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was jointly awarded to Eric Betzig, Stefan W. Hell and William E. Moerner for the development of super-resolved fluorescence microscopy.

questions.question: The Land Boundary Agreement between India and Bangladesh was ratified through the:
questions.explanation: The India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement was implemented via the Constitution (100th Amendment) Act, 2015, enabling exchange of enclaves between the two countries.

questions.question: The sixty-eighth session of the World Health Assembly (WHA) took place in ___________, 18-26 May 2015.
questions.explanation: The World Health Assembly, the decision-making body of the WHO, is held annually in Geneva, Switzerland - including its 68th session in May 2015.

questions.question: What term is used for the maximum capital which a company can raise in its lifetime (as per its incorporation documents)?
questions.explanation: The maximum capital a company can raise is known variously as Authorized Capital, Registered Capital or Nominal Capital - these are different names for the same concept as stated in the company's Memorandum of Association.

questions.question: Which state government approved mandatory Global Positioning System (GPS) devices in all public transport vehicles from June 2015?
questions.explanation: The Delhi government mandated GPS devices (along with panic buttons) in all public transport vehicles from June 2015, as a passenger-safety measure.

questions.question: China signed a currency swap deal with which country (around 2015)?
questions.explanation: China signed a yuan-peso currency swap agreement with Chile in 2015, part of a broader push to internationalize the renminbi.

questions.question: The concept of 'Universal Banking' was implemented in India on the recommendations of:
questions.explanation: The R H Khan Committee (1997-98) recommended a move towards Universal Banking, where banks offer a full range of financial services including those traditionally done by development finance institutions.

questions.question: Who headed the committee formed by SEBI to frame a single set of guidelines for all types of foreign investors?
questions.explanation: The K M Chandrashekhar Committee was set up to recommend rationalising and harmonising the various categories of foreign portfolio/institutional investors under a single framework.

questions.question: The largest shareholder (by percentage shareholding) of a nationalized bank is:
questions.explanation: Nationalized (public sector) banks are majority-owned by the Government of India, which holds the largest shareholding stake in them.

questions.question: Which of the following organizations finances the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF)?
questions.explanation: The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund is administered and financed by NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development), funded via contributions from banks that fall short of their priority-sector lending targets.

questions.question: Who is the author of the book 'Odyssey of My Life'?
questions.explanation: Per the answer key, 'Odyssey of My Life' is credited to Shivraj V Patil, the former Union Home Minister.

questions.question: World Photography Day is observed on:
questions.explanation: World Photography Day is observed every year on 19th August, commemorating the invention of the daguerreotype photographic process.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements on Islamic banking is incorrect?
(A) Islamic banking is only for Muslims
(B) Islamic banking activity does not allow paying and receiving of interest
(C) Islamic banking promotes the principle of profit sharing between the banking institution and the depositor
questions.explanation: Statement A is incorrect - Islamic banking follows Shariah-compliant principles but its products can be, and are, used by customers of any faith, not exclusively Muslims. Statements B (no interest) and C (profit-sharing) are correct descriptions of Islamic banking.

questions.question:
The difference between the outflow and inflow of foreign currency (on account of current transactions) is known as:
(A) Foreign Exchange Reserves
(B) Current Account Deficit
(C) Fiscal Deficit
(D) Balance of Payments
questions.explanation: The gap between a country's outflow and inflow of foreign currency from current (trade, services, transfer) transactions is termed the Current Account Deficit.

questions.question: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) established JLGs to extract productive capability from the rural population. JLG stands for:
questions.explanation: JLG stands for Joint Liability Group, an informal group of individuals who come together to avail bank credit through mutual guarantee, as promoted by NABARD.

questions.question: What is MZM in the money market?
questions.explanation: MZM (Money of Zero Maturity) is a monetary aggregate that measures the supply of financial assets redeemable at par on demand, without a maturity period.

questions.question: The long term objective of marketing is:
questions.explanation: Sustainable marketing aims for profit maximization achieved through customer satisfaction, not profit alone or satisfaction alone.

questions.question: Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) means:
options: each year, budgeting starts from a scratch
questions.explanation: In zero-based budgeting, every budgeting cycle starts from a 'zero base' - every expense must be justified afresh each year rather than simply carried forward from the previous year's budget.

questions.question: A marketing technique where the marketer plays a specific role in a particular segment is called:
questions.explanation: Focusing on a specific, well-defined segment of the market is known as niche marketing.

questions.question: In the Marketing Mix, the 4 P's imply:
questions.explanation: The classic Marketing Mix 4 P's are Product, Price, Place and Promotion.

questions.question: Good marketing strategy envisages good and proper ___________.
questions.explanation: Good marketing strategy, especially in services like banking, centres on effective relationship management with customers.

questions.question: Marketing in banks has been necessitated due to:
questions.explanation: Globalisation opened Indian banking to competition from foreign and private players, making active marketing necessary for banks to retain and grow their customer base.

questions.question: Innovation in marketing is the same as:
questions.explanation: Marketing innovation is fundamentally driven by creativity - devising new ideas, products or approaches.

questions.question: Effective Selling Skills depend on:
options: Number of languages known to the DSA
questions.explanation: Effective selling depends primarily on a salesperson's knowledge of the related market - understanding customer needs, competing products and market conditions.

questions.question: The first CNG train was launched on which section?
questions.explanation: India's first CNG-fitted train was launched on the Rewari-Rohtak section in Haryana, run by Northern Railway.

questions.question: As reported around 2015, name the Malaysian woman claimed to be among the world's oldest living persons.
questions.explanation: Per the answer key, this refers to a Malaysian woman, Yati Musdi, reported in the press around this time as a claimant to extreme old age; such regional longevity claims are often not independently verified by bodies like Guinness World Records.

questions.question: Which of the following was the theme of World Health Day 2015?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization's theme for World Health Day 2015 (7 April) was 'Food Safety'.
